prompt: Why is a point-in-time recovery better than lesson 2's dump for this mistake?
hint: What happens to the orders written between the backup and the DELETE?

choices.text: It restores faster than a dump of the same size
choices.why: It may, but speed is not what this mistake needed.

choices.text: It can bring back the orders written after the DELETE too, without a repair
choices.why: Anything after the target is not in the copy; that is what the repair is for.

choices.text: It keeps every change made before the mistake
choices.why: Right. The dump would have lost everything between its snapshot and the DELETE.

choices.text: It does not need a backup at all, only the log
choices.why: Replay starts from a base backup; the log alone has nowhere to start.

prompt: Right after noticing the mistake, why ask which segment is being written now?
hint: The mistake is seconds old.

choices.text: Because it is where the mistake is
choices.why: Right. A mistake from the last few seconds is in the current segment, so that is where pg_waldump looks.

choices.text: To delete that segment before it is archived
choices.why: Deleting log would break the archive and lose the good transactions in it too.

choices.text: To know how many bytes the DELETE took up in the log
choices.why: Size is not the question; finding the transaction is.

choices.text: Because a restore can only target the current segment
choices.why: A restore can target any point after the backup.

prompt: How many orders did the mistaken `DELETE` remove?
hint: It reported it.

prompt: What did `awk '/desc: DELETE/ {print $8}' | sort | uniq -c` count, over the segment's dump?
hint: Field 8 of a record line is the transaction id.

choices.text: DELETE statements per table in the database
choices.why: pg_waldump knows records, not statements; and the count was by transaction.

choices.text: Commits per second during the day
choices.why: Commits are COMMIT records; the filter picked DELETE records.

choices.text: Segments of log written by each session
choices.why: Nothing in the dump is counted per session.

choices.text: Deleted rows per transaction
choices.why: Right. One transaction, 742, deleted 12059 rows, the number the DELETE reported.

prompt: Which transaction id did the `DELETE` have?
hint: The one with 12059 rows.

prompt: `pg_waldump` printed `error in WAL record … invalid record length … expected at least 24, got 0` before its results. What does it mean here?
hint: Is the segment finished?

choices.text: The segment is corrupt and the restore will fail
choices.why: Nothing is damaged; the restore later used this segment.

choices.text: It hit the end of a segment in use
choices.why: Right: it read to the end of what was written, in a segment still in use. The rest of the 16 MB file is still empty, so the dump stops there and says so.

choices.text: The DELETE was too large to log
choices.why: All 12059 rows were logged and counted.

choices.text: It needs to run as postgres, not with sudo
choices.why: It ran with sudo and read the file; the message is about the content.

prompt: On a busy server, a segment holds thousands of transactions and several large ones. What narrows the search to the mistake?
hint: pg_waldump has options for this.

choices.text: Restoring once per transaction until the data looks right
choices.why: That works in principle and takes a restore per guess.

choices.text: Its --relation, --start and --end options
choices.why: Right: --relation for the table, --start and --end for the stretch of log you know. Roughly when, and which table, cut a busy segment to a handful of candidates.

choices.text: Reading the server's log, which records every statement by default
choices.why: By default PostgreSQL does not log statements.

choices.text: Picking the transaction with the most records
choices.why: On a busy server, the biggest transaction is often a legitimate batch.

prompt: The first restore stopped with `recovery ended before configured recovery target was reached`. Why?
hint: Which segment held transaction 742, and was it in the archive?

choices.text: The xid was mistyped
choices.why: The target was 742, the right one; the second attempt used the same.

choices.text: --target-exclusive is not allowed with an xid
choices.why: It is allowed, and the second attempt used it.

choices.text: The base backup was too old to reach that point
choices.why: Age does not stop replay; a missing segment does.

choices.text: The segment with the target was not archived yet
choices.why: Right. 742 was in …04, still being written, and the archive ended at …03.

prompt: Why does the lesson call that refusal good news?
hint: What would the alternative have been?

choices.text: A wrong copy would have looked right
choices.why: Right. A copy silently stopped at …03 would have looked recovered and lacked the five good orders, and nobody would have known.

choices.text: Because it proves the backup is valid
choices.why: It proves nothing about the backup; it is about the target.

choices.text: Because it means the live server is still running
choices.why: The refusal says nothing about the live server.

choices.text: Because it deleted the restored copy automatically
choices.why: The copy was left as it was; the next attempt removed it by hand.

prompt: What made the target segment reach the archive?
hint: Lesson 4.

choices.text: A restart of the restored server
choices.why: The restored server reads the archive; it cannot add to it, and its archiving was off.

choices.text: pgbackrest check on the restored server
choices.why: check runs against the stanza's own server, and the segment had to come from the live one.

choices.text: pg_switch_wal() on the live server
choices.why: Right. It finished …04, and archive-push sent it.

choices.text: Waiting for the next full backup
choices.why: That would have archived it too, eventually; the fix was immediate.

prompt: Match each recovery target with when to use it.
hint: One of them needs preparation in advance.

pairs.right: The log has shown you which transaction
You know roughly when, and nothing more precise
You have a position in the log rather than a transaction
Somebody created a restore point before the change

right_distractors: You want the latest moment the archive holds

prompt: What does `--target-action=pause` give you that `promote` does not?
hint: Read-only, waiting.

choices.text: A faster recovery
choices.why: It is the same replay; it just waits at the end.

choices.text: Writes allowed while paused
choices.why: A paused server is still in recovery, read-only.

choices.text: Automatic repair of the live database
choices.why: Nothing touches the live database.

choices.text: A look at the copy before anything is decided
choices.why: Right. If the target was wrong, you restore again with nothing lost.

prompt: How many orders did the paused copy hold?
hint: Fifty thousand, plus the orders before the DELETE.

prompt: A team is about to run a migration that rewrites a large table. What is the cheapest thing to do first, for recovery's sake?
hint: Make a future target exact.

choices.text: Take a full base backup and wait for it
choices.why: Useful and slow; the archive already lets you return to any moment after the last backup.

choices.text: Switch archiving off during the migration
choices.why: That removes the very log you would recover with.

choices.text: Run SELECT pg_create_restore_point('before-migration')
choices.why: Right. One call, and recovery_target_name gives an exact target if the migration goes wrong.

choices.text: Pause replication
choices.why: Replication is lesson 11; it does not make a recovery target exact.

prompt: After the restored server was promoted, `pg_control_checkpoint()` reported timeline 2. Why a new timeline?
hint: Two histories now continue from one point.

choices.text: A new history began where replay stopped
choices.why: Right. Recovery stopped before the end of the log, so a new history began there: timeline 2 left timeline 1 before transaction 742.

choices.text: Every restart increases the timeline
choices.why: A restart keeps the timeline; only a recovery that ends before the end of the log forks it.

choices.text: pgBackRest numbers each restore
choices.why: The timeline is PostgreSQL's, written by the server at promotion.

choices.text: The live server moved to timeline 2 when the copy was made
choices.why: The live server is still on timeline 1.

prompt: The file that records where timeline 2 left timeline 1 is called `00000002.___`.
hint: It records the fork.

prompt: In `000000020000000000000005`, what do the first eight digits say?
hint: Compare it with …0004 on timeline 1.

choices.text: The server's port
choices.why: Ports are not in segment names.

choices.text: The timeline the segment belongs to
choices.why: Right. Same position in the log, a different history, a different name.

choices.text: The day of the month it was written
choices.why: Segment names carry no dates.

choices.text: The size of the segment in megabytes
choices.why: Every segment is 16 MB; the name does not say so.

prompt: When is replacing the live database with the restored copy the right choice, rather than repairing from it?
hint: What happens to everything after the target?

choices.text: Whenever the copy holds more rows than the live database
choices.why: Row counts do not decide it; trust in what came after does.

choices.text: When the mistake was a DELETE rather than an UPDATE
choices.why: Either can be repaired from a copy.

choices.text: When nothing after it is trustworthy
choices.why: Right, or when the live server is gone. Otherwise replacing throws away every good write since the mistake.

choices.text: When the restore took less than an hour
choices.why: Speed does not change what replacing loses.

prompt: How many orders did the live shop hold after the repair?
hint: Fifty thousand, five before, three after.

prompt: A support agent says the mistake happened "at 16:36" by the clock on their laptop, in another city. What should the time target be built from?
hint: Whose clock wrote the commit times?

choices.text: The commit times pg_waldump shows, with their offset
choices.why: Right. The database's own record of when each transaction committed is the clock that counts.

choices.text: The agent's time, converted to the server's zone
choices.why: Better than unconverted, and still a laptop clock; the log has the real time.

choices.text: The agent's time minus one hour, to be safe
choices.why: Going earlier is safer, but an hour loses good transactions for nothing.

choices.text: The time the monitoring system showed the drop
choices.why: Another clock again, and later than the commit.

prompt: Why is a target that is too early safer than one that is too late?
hint: Which of the two can the repair fix?

choices.text: Too early is faster to replay
choices.why: Slightly, and that is not the reason.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses targets after the last commit
choices.why: It refuses targets it cannot reach, which is a different problem.

choices.text: Too late damages the archive
choices.why: Replay never writes to the archive.

choices.text: Only too late replays the mistake
choices.why: Right. Too early loses changes the repair can bring back from the live server; too late replays the mistake. Missing good changes can be copied from the live server; a replayed mistake makes the copy useless.

prompt: Put the steps of a point-in-time recovery in order.
hint: Find the moment before restoring to it.
items: Find the target transaction or time in the log
Make sure the archive holds the segment with the target
Restore to a separate server with archiving off, paused at the target
Check the copy, then promote and replace or repair
trap: A target you have not found cannot be restored to; a segment not archived makes the restore fail; and nothing is decided until the paused copy has been checked.

prompt: A restore to `recovery_target_time = '16:36:09'` produced a copy with 37952 orders. What happened?
hint: The DELETE committed at 16:36:08.563.

choices.text: The archive is missing a segment
choices.why: A missing segment would make recovery stop with an error, not give a copy past the mistake.

choices.text: The target was after the DELETE, so it was replayed
choices.why: Right. 37952 is the shop with the DELETE and three later orders; the target must be earlier than 16:36:08.563.

choices.text: The copy is correct, and the count includes old orders twice
choices.why: Old orders are what is missing, not doubled.

choices.text: Time targets ignore DELETE statements
choices.why: Replay applies every record before the target, DELETEs included.
